t.1.184.1: Vaiśaṃpāyana said: Then Dhṛṣṭadyumna, the Pāñcāla prince, followed from behind the two delights of the Kurus as they went to the dwelling of the Bhārgava.
t.1.184.3: Then in the evening Bhīma, the crusher of foes, Jiṣṇu, and the illustrious twins, having gone about begging alms, presented them to Yudhiṣṭhira, they whose spirits were undaunted.
t.1.184.2: Unrecognized, he stationed men all around, and he himself took up a position close by, at the dwelling of the Bhārgava.
t.1.184.4: Then the generous Kuntī, at the proper time, spoke these words to the daughter of Drupada: “Take the first portion from this, good lady, and make the bali offering, and give alms to the brahmin.”
t.1.184.6: And give half to Bhīma, good lady, this one here whose form is like that of a rutting bull, the dark youth endowed with a powerful build, for this hero is always a great eater.
t.1.184.5: Give food to those who desire it, the people who have sought shelter all around us. Then quickly divide what remains, and set aside half for the four, for me, and for yourself.
t.1.184.8: The swift and mighty Sahadeva, son of Mādrī, made a bed of kuśa grass on the ground; then all the heroes, each spreading out his own deerskin, slept upon the earth.
t.1.184.7: The princess, joyful in her looks and not doubting that her words were good, did exactly as she had been told, the virtuous woman; and they all ate the food.
t.1.184.9: The heads of those best of the Kurus lay toward the quarter ruled by Agastya; Kuntī was placed above their heads, and Kṛṣṇā lay crosswise at their feet.
t.1.184.10: She lay on the ground with the sons of Pāṇḍu on the kuśa grass, placed as though she were a pillow for their feet. She felt no sorrow there, nor did she look down on those bulls among the Kurus.
t.1.184.11: There the heroes told varied tales concerning armies, of divine weapons, of chariots and elephants, of swords, maces, and battle-axes.
t.1.184.13: But the prince Dhṛṣṭadyumna, intending to report to King Drupada in full all that had happened with them and all that had been said during the night, went off in haste.
t.1.184.14: But the great-souled king of the Pāñcālas, dejected in appearance and unable to find the Pāṇḍavas, questioned Dhṛṣṭadyumna: "Where has she gone? By whom has Kṛṣṇā been taken away?"
t.1.184.12: The son of the Pāñcāla king then heard those talks of theirs as they were being recounted, and of Kṛṣṇā lying there thus; and all those men saw her as well.
t.1.184.15: I hope she has not been won by a śūdra, nor by one of low birth, nor by a tribute-paying vaiśya? I hope no foot has been smeared upon my head, and I hope the garland has not fallen upon a cremation ground?
t.1.184.16: Was it, I hope, an eminent man of equal class, or perhaps even one of higher class who came here? I hope, son, that no left foot has been planted on my head today through the touching of Kṛṣṇā.
t.1.184.17: And shall I perhaps, supremely delighted, offer sacrifice after being joined in alliance with Pārtha, that bull among men? Tell me truly: who is that illustrious one who has won my daughter today?
t.1.184.18: Are the sons of Vicitravīrya, that foremost hero of the Kurus, still alive today? And was it the younger Pārtha who today took up the bow and struck down the target?
